1:
Ellicott opens with the question no one else asks: where did this story come from? No eye-witness was present, so it must be myth, supernatural revelation, or Christ's own account of himself. He rejects the first — a legend built on Genesis 3 would have kept the serpent and the trees, and the expected Messiah was "a great and mighty king", never "a sufferer tried and tempted". He rejects the second because the evangelists are compilers, and the differing order of the temptations tells "against the idea of a supernatural revelation". What remains is that Jesus told a disciple.

How he was led is disputed by degree. Robertson notes Mark's verb drives is stronger, and reads "a strong impulsion by the Holy Spirit" sending Jesus out to think through what his baptism had committed him to. Ellicott goes further. Gathering the analogous cases — John in the Spirit, Ezekiel lifted up, Philip caught away — he concludes it was "more or less of the nature of ecstasy, in which the ordinary phenomena of consciousness and animal life were in great measure suspended". Pseudo-Chrysostom makes it a second baptism: baptised by John in water, he is led out "to be baptized by the fire of temptation".

Several frame it as an old quarrel resumed. Lightfoot dates it exactly: "the war, proclaimed of old in Eden between the serpent, and the seed of the serpent, and the seed of the woman" now takes the field, the devil, knowing whom he faced, taking "a more hardened boldness than ever". Clarke makes the same link to the bruising of the serpent's head, noting that "the first act of the ministry of Jesus Christ was a combat with Satan". Henry calls it "a famous duel, fought hand to hand, between Michael and the dragon", the heel bruised and the head broken.

Why God permits the assault draws out Chrysostom, who gives five reasons: to prove the tempted man stronger than he knew, to keep him modest under great gifts, to convince the demon he has been truly forsaken, to temper him "better than any steel", and to demonstrate the treasures entrusted to him. His premise is encouraging — "the devil would not have assailed thee, unless he had seen thee brought to greater honor", as with Adam and Job. Henry draws the practical form from the word then: high privilege is no security, and "the enriched soul must double its guard". Wesley: after the clearest light, expect the sharpest temptation.

On the forty days all reach for Moses and Elijah, and Barnes settles whether Christ ate by Luke's flat "he ate nothing", placing the angels' ministry at the close. Clarke quotes the rabbis: asked how any man could fast so long, Rabbi Meir answered that in any city one lives by its customs, and Moses "ascended to heaven, where they neither eat nor drink". Lightfoot alone supplies a calendar: mid-Tisri onward, October into November, so that Jesus "conflicted with cold, as well as want and Satan".

Whether he felt hunger throughout is a real question. Gill finds it "very surprising" that none attended the whole time, and Robertson quotes Alford that "the wants of the natural body were suspended". Ellicott takes the closing words as "a partial return to the common life of sensation", the cravings giving the tempter his opening. Calvin makes the point serve a polemic: there was no virtue of abstinence in refusing food "for which he had no more appetite than if he had not been clothed with flesh".

From which Calvin turns on Lent. To appoint a forty days' fast in imitation of Christ "is mere folly", since neither Moses nor Christ kept such a fast yearly but once in a lifetime, and the imitators "stuff their belly so completely at dinner, that, when the hour of supper arrives, they have no difficulty in abstaining from food."
3:
Whether anything was there to see divides them. Gill has the devil tempting secretly for forty days and then, that failing, putting "on a visible form, and with an articulate, audible voice"; Wesley guesses "probably in a human shape, as one that desired to inquire farther into the evidences of his being the Messiah". Ellicott refuses the picture: nothing suggests "a bodily presence visible to the eye of sense", and attempts to supply one — Milton's, or the rationalists' scribe or priest — are "unauthorised, and diminish our sense of the reality and mystery of the Temptation".

Both grammarians notice Son of God lacks its article, and read the omission oppositely. Clarke concludes the devil was probing: "whatever Satan might suspect, he did not fully know that the person he tempted was the true Messiah. Perhaps one grand object of his temptation was to find this out." Robertson takes the conditional as assuming its own truth: the devil quotes the baptismal voice back at him and dares him to act on it.

The stones are realised vividly: Ellicott hears the demonstrative "as if in union with glance and gesture", pointing at "the loaf-like flints of the Jordan desert", and Robertson imagines the devil holding one up. "It was all so simple, obvious, easy."

What sin was urged is where Calvin loses patience with the tradition. The ancients, he says, "amused themselves with ingenious trifles" by making the three temptations gluttony, ambition and covetousness — but nothing is intemperate in a starving man wanting food, and "what luxury will they fancy themselves to have discovered in the use of bread?" His own answer: "Satan made a direct attack on the faith of Christ", hoping that once faith fell he might be driven to unlawful means. Clarke states it in a sentence: "distrust the Divine providence and support, and make use of illicit means to supply thy necessities."

Ellicott alone makes the temptation layered. Part he compares to Esau's "what profit shall this birthright do to me?"; part is inference, since Sonship might carry a lordship over nature; part is public. The thought came and was rejected as "an act of self-assertion and distrust", denying rather than affirming the Sonship just declared.

On the answer from Deuteronomy three voices reject a reading nobody in the passage holds. Barnes insists neither Moses nor Christ "had any reference to spiritual food", the Hebrew word meaning thing; Gill grants the spiritual sense is "a certain truth" but not the meaning here; Calvin says some "torture it to a false meaning". What it means, all three agree, is that God is not tied to bread — manna proved it. Clarke pushes further: even fasting at God's command "becomes a mean of supporting that life which it seems naturally calculated to impair".

Ellicott asks instead where the words came from. All three answers are drawn from two chapters of Deuteronomy, one worn in the phylacteries, so they had been familiar since childhood — and with them, he suggests, Jesus "may have sustained the faith of others in the struggles of the Nazareth home with poverty and want". Jamieson thinks no passage in the Old Testament "could have been pitched upon more apposite", since Israel spent forty years in a waste wilderness "not starving, but divinely provided for", and puts the conclusion in Christ's mouth: "as man, therefore, I will await divine supply." Robertson notes only that Deuteronomy answers the devil every time. Calvin turns it into a weapon: Christ "uses Scripture as his shield", and those who withhold Scripture from the people "deprive them of their arms, by which alone their safety could be preserved". Pseudo-Chrysostom offers the pastoral form: the devil despaired at the fast and took heart at the hunger, so if tempted after fasting, "say not, I have lost the fruit of my fast".
5:
Matthew and Luke order the last two temptations differently, and those who notice take three attitudes. Ellicott adjudicates: either Luke's informant was less accurate, or the impressions left on those who received the account differed, especially if the temptations recurred; on balance Matthew's order "seems the truest", since "Get thee behind me, Satan" belongs at the close. Robertson simply explains Luke's principle, which is geographical. Calvin refuses the question — the evangelists did not set out to preserve exact order, so which contest came second "need not give us much trouble or uneasiness".

Whether Christ was physically carried divides them four ways. Gill is unhesitating: it happened "not in a visionary way, but really and truly", Satan by divine permission and Christ's consent having power to move his body, as the Spirit caught away Philip. Barnes denies it flatly — "there is no evidence that Satan had power to do any of these things" — and shows from parallels that the verb means only to conduct or accompany. Ellicott reads the Ezekiel visions instead and puts the taking "outside the conditions of local motion", borrowing Paul's formula: whether in the body or out of it we cannot say. Calvin, noting that the showing of all the kingdoms "agrees better with the idea of a vision", declines to settle it: "in a matter that is doubtful, and where ignorance brings no risk, I choose rather to suspend my judgment."

Where the pinnacle stood is guessed rather than known. Lightfoot admits it "is in vain to seek, because it cannot be found", then proposes the porch or the royal gallery. Barnes rules out the roof, since Josephus says it was set with golden spikes to keep birds off, and settles on the southern porch; Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all name Herod's portico. On its height they differ without noticing: Barnes makes the drop more than seven hundred feet, Ellicott four hundred cubits, Robertson about four hundred and fifty — agreeing only that one could not look down without dizziness. Barnes adds the etymology: the word belongs to birds, the porch being a wing "because it resembled a bird dropping its wings".

Lightfoot brings up something from the Talmud that bears on nothing and is hard to forget. The priests went up by stairs to the temple roof, and when fire was first set to the Temple threw the keys of its chambers towards heaven, saying "O thou eternal Lord, because we are not worthy to keep these keys, to thee they are delivered." A shape like a hand came from heaven and took them; then they leapt into the fire.

Ellicott and Robertson both record a grim coincidence: James the Lord's brother is said to have been thrown from this same pinnacle into the court below.

What was urged Ellicott states by exclusion. The point was not a public wonder before the worshippers to win power and popularity; the answer given shows the suggestion "tended, not to vain glory, but to distrust simulating reliance". Calvin sees the same shape as the mirror of the first attack: having failed to drive Christ to despair for want of bread, Satan now "exhorts him to indulge a foolish and vain confidence... to throw himself, without necessity, into manifest danger". Neither despair nor presumption is permitted; we may not be discouraged by want, "neither are we at liberty to raise our crests, or ascend higher than God permits us".

Pseudo-Chrysostom supplies the devil's reasoning between rounds. From the first answer he "could learn nothing certain whether He were God or man", so revised his estimate downward — perhaps merely a holy man who has subdued the flesh — and changed his line accordingly. Ellicott adds the memory the place would have carried: Jesus had visited Jerusalem before, and "in past years He may have looked down from that portico on the dark gorge beneath".
6:
Clarke notices what makes this attack different: the answer that defeated the last becomes the ground of this one. Christ repelled the first by confidence in God's goodness, "and now Satan solicits him to make trial of it" — so "the very means we make use of to repel one temptation may be used by him as the groundwork of another".

The quotation is doctored. Clarke names the surgery: the clause to keep thee in all thy ways "Satan chose to leave out, as quite unsuitable to his design". Robertson lists the technique — "the devil quotes the Word of God, misinterprets it, omits a clause, and tries to trip the Son of God by the Word of God" — and calls it a skilful thrust. Calvin's image is stronger: the misapplication aims at "rendering life deadly to Christ, and of converting bread into poison".

That image raises the obvious objection, which Calvin meets. If Scripture can be turned to such use, should we not distrust it? "Nor ought we to imitate the madness of those who throw away Scripture, as if it admitted of every kind of interpretation, because the devil misapplies it. For the same reason, we ought to abstain from food, to avoid the risk of being poisoned." Christ does not let the enemy "seize and carry off the Scripture, with which he formerly armed himself", but quotes back.

Where the fallacy sits Calvin locates with care. Satan "is not wrong in proving from this passage, that angels have been given to Christ, to wait on him and to guard him". The fraud is the omitted condition: the guardianship is promised to those who "keep themselves within their bounds, and walk in their ways", God commands the walking and then promises the angels; Satan produces the angels to license a leap. Clarke says it shorter: "as the path of duty is the way of safety, they are entitled to no good when they walk out of it."

Clarke reads the promise with unexpected tenderness: bearing up in the hands is "a metaphor taken from a nurse's management of her child: in teaching it to walk, she guides it along plain ground; but, when stones or other obstacles occur, she lifts up the child, and carries it over them, and then sets it down to walk again". Ellicott adds a preposition: better on the hands than in.

Robertson supplies the physical and public dimensions others pass over. The height "would intensify the nervous dread that most people feel", and a man seen "sailing down as if from heaven" would satisfy what the populace expected of a Messiah. The angels "would be a spiritual parachute for Christ". Ellicott had rejected that reading outright, holding the suggestion tended not to display but to distrust.

Ellicott notices which words were used against him: the verses turned into a snare "must have been precisely those that had before been most precious" — words Jesus had fed on and found "the stay and comfort of His life", without dreaming of testing them by devices of his own. The answer, from the chapter he likely wore in his phylactery, carries a history: Massah, where the sin was refusing to believe God present until shown a proof. To demand one now would have been to join them.

Gill sees a further restraint. Christ "takes no notice of the false and wrong citation of scripture made by the devil", setting another text against it instead of arguing. Calvin explains why that settles it: promises cannot be claimed apart from commands, and those who abandon the means God gives "act as absurdly as if one were to cut off a man's arms and hands, and then order him to work". Wesley adds only that the bearing up means great care; Ellicott hears the same submission in the twelve legions never asked for.
8:
Pseudo-Chrysostom reads the three assaults as nets: Christ "had broken the nets of appetite, had passed over those of ambition, he now spreads for Him those of covetousness" — the threefold scheme Calvin elsewhere dismissed as ingenious trifles. He adds that the higher the mountain the wider the view, and supposes the devil had noted this one while going about the earth.

Which mountain nobody claims to know. Gill says the question "is not of any moment; nor can it be known", while reporting the guess of Lebanon; Robertson wonders whether it was Quarantania. What matters is not where he stood but what he saw.

Barnes and Clarke both take the sight literally, and both reach for the same traveller. The Abbé Mariti described a summit overlooking "the mountains of Arabia, the country of Gilead, the plains of Moab, the plains of Jericho, the river Jordan, and the whole extent of the Dead Sea" — enough, they think, so that "we must not suppose that there was any miracle when they were shown". This requires the world to mean Judea, and both argue it: the land was divided into three governments whose rulers are called kings in the Gospels, and Clarke suspects Matthew wrote the Hebrew word meaning equally the earth and the land. His reason is blunt — no mountain could show one hemisphere, "and the other must of necessity be in darkness".

Lightfoot answers the same question entirely differently: the kingdoms of the world means Rome and her empire. He gives four reasons — that empire is called "all the world" by sacred and profane writers alike, other cities counted for little beside it, no part of the earth had standing outside it, and Rome was "the seat of Satan". What was offered was the pomp and power of Caesar, and Lightfoot adds the sequel: "this, antichrist afterward obtained."

Ellicott treats the verse as settling the Temptation's whole nature. If proof were wanted, here it is: all of it "was in the region of which the spirit, and not the senses, takes cognisance", since no mountain commands such a survey; and Luke's "in a moment of time" he calls a flash "which concentrate[s] into a single act of consciousness the work of years". Wesley agrees in five words, "a kind of visionary representation". Having brushed Milton aside earlier, Ellicott half recommends him here: the expansion in Paradise Regained is "too obviously the work of a scholar exulting in his scholarship", yet the first serious attempt to imagine what was set before Christ's mind.

Jamieson notices only what Matthew leaves out: Luke adds "and the glory of them", which Matthew, "having already said that this was showed Him, did not need to repeat". Robertson declines to make the two accounts exclusive. The panorama "had to be partially mental and imaginative", but "this fact does not prove that all phases of the temptations were subjective without any objective presence of the devil. Both could be true."

Calvin holds the two together differently, in the chapter's most careful distinction. The effect on Christ's eyes was real, owed not to weakness in his nature but "to a voluntary dispensation and permission". Then the point: "while his senses were moved and powerfully affected by the glory of the kingdoms which was presented to them, no inward desire arose in his mind". With us the lusts of the flesh "like wild beasts, are drawn, and hurry us along"; Christ "had the same feelings with ourselves, but he had no irregular appetites".

The offer itself Calvin treats as theft. In claiming to bestow the kingdoms the devil is "robbing God of the government of the world, and claiming it for himself" — and the fraud still works, since men who profess that every good comes from God nonetheless "make Satan the distributor of all the riches in the world".
9:
The startling thing is how many concede the offer was real. Barnes allows the claim "with considerable justice", the kingdoms being wicked; Ellicott says it "rested on the apparent evidence of the world's history", where Herods and Caesars rose by trampling God's law, and grants that "in part, the claim is allowed by our Lord's language". Robertson agrees "Jesus does not deny the grip of the devil on the world of men", spurning only the condition. Calvin alone treats the claim as theft.

What is appealed to has changed. Ellicott notes the temptation "is no longer addressed to the sense of Sonship, but to the love of power" — to be a king like other kings, delivering his people and achieving the promised glory, if only he stepped outside his Father's limits. Robertson borrows McNeile: a temporal rather than spiritual dominion, gained at once, by homage that "would make the self-constituted Messiah the vice-regent of the devil and not of God".

Whether the reply was "get thee hence" or "get thee behind me" divides them four ways. Gill reports the second reading in some copies; Clarke says it is added "by a multitude of the best MSS., Versions, and Fathers"; Robertson denies it — those words "belong to Matthew 16:23, not here". Wesley makes the difference one of meaning: behind me would send Satan to his proper place, as it later sent Peter, whereas this is dismissal. Calvin refuses to speculate "as if the same words had not been addressed to Satan" — while Ellicott builds on precisely that identity, Peter, trying to turn his master from suffering, having renewed this temptation and met the self-same words.

Why the tone hardens is answered with unusual agreement. Barnes observes the earlier attacks were plausible and not directly against God's law; this is "a more decided and deadly thrust". Ellicott makes the changed formula the evidence: before, "Evil had presented itself in disguise, making sins of distrust appear as acts of faith, while now it showed itself in its naked and absolute antagonism to the divine will". Wesley notices Christ now uses the enemy's own name, "which he had not done before"; Gill, that mildness was shown until the behaviour became intolerable.

Calvin takes the answer as settling a later argument. Rome, he says, concedes latreia to God alone but keeps an inferior douleia for "dead men, and on their bones and statues" — a distinction Christ destroys by claiming for God the word meaning bodily homage, so "not only the inward worship, but also the outward manifestation of it, is due to God alone". Ellicott notes without polemic that the word means homage offered a king rather than adoration due to God, and Robertson that Luke's softer "worship before me" came to the same thing.

Clarke sums the conflict as four attacks — distrust, presumption, worldly ambition, idolatry, "there is probably not a temptation of Satan, but is reducible to one or other of these four articles" — and draws the consolation that being tempted, while one resists, is not sin, Christ having been tempted to worship the devil.

What the angels did divides gently. Clarke and Wesley have them bring food, Wesley adding they came "to congratulate his victory", Robertson that they cheered him in "the inevitable nervous and spiritual reaction from the strain of conflict". Ellicott declines to specify, warning against "sensualising it as poets and artists have done", and adds that their service came "as the reward of the abnegation which refused to make their ministry the subject of an experimental test". Cyril presses the verb: Scripture "saith not, they succoured Him, but they ministered unto Him, that is, like servants" — proof that the Son is Lord of angels. Calvin adds that Christ was never forsaken by them, the grace present with him being "sometimes hidden, so far as respects the feeling of the flesh".
12:
A year disappears between one verse and the next, and several stop to say what fell into it. Ellicott lists the gap's contents from the fourth Gospel: the return to the Baptist and the call of the first disciples, Cana, the cleansing of the Temple, Nicodemus, the Baptist's last testimony, then the imprisonment and the journey back through Samaria. Henry gives much the same list; Wesley traces the itinerary step by step and insists "this journey was not immediately after his temptation". Robertson calls the omitted stretch "the year of obscurity", borrowing Stalker, and observes that without John's Gospel we should know nothing of it.

Ellicott draws a further inference. Since the verse explains the move to Galilee by John's arrest, it implies a preceding ministry in Judaea "which for some reason the writer does not narrate" — a silence deliberate rather than ignorant.

Calvin faces the resulting difficulty: John's Gospel has the Baptist and Christ teaching at once, which looks like a contradiction of the sequence here. He answers that the three evangelists pass over the overlap because the Baptist's course was preparatory and unfinished, so that although Christ taught within that period "he did not, strictly speaking, begin to [teach] till he succeeded to John". The image he ends on carries the argument: "when the dawn was passed, the sun arose."

Why he withdrew at all is answered three ways. Chrysostom takes it as instruction — Christ departs "again instructing us not to go to meet temptations, but to give place and withdraw ourselves. For it is no reproach, the not casting one's self into danger, but the failing to stand manfully when fallen into it." Barnes denies the safety motive outright, since Jesus went straight into Herod's territory having given him no offence, and substitutes three others: the people's attention had been roused by John, John's work needed seconding, and beginning near Jerusalem would have drawn the envy of scribes and priests too soon. Henry takes both at once — Christ went "not only to provide for his own safety" but "to supply the want of John Baptist, and to build upon the good foundation he had laid".

Chrysostom then notices a larger pattern. "Mark how in every case when He is about to depart unto the Gentiles, He hath the occasion given Him by Jews" — here by plotting against the forerunner they "thrust out Christ into the Galilee of the Gentiles". The prophecy's darkness he takes as moral, not physical: not sensible darkness but "men's errors and ungodliness", answered by a light called great because it was true.

Henry is most interested in the timing, and makes the two ministries a matter of deliberate arrangement. Christ did not move until John was silenced, because otherwise "the minds of people would have been distracted between the two; one would have said, I am of John, and another, I am of Jesus. John must be Christ's harbinger, but not his rival." Hence his figure: "the moon and stars are lost when the sun rises." The same providence secures the succession — when God removes one instrument he raises another: "Moses my servant is dead, John is cast into prison; now, therefore, Joshua, arise; Jesus, arise." Nor will he let the imprisonment pass as circumstance: "if John be cast into prison, Jesus hears it, takes cognizance of it, and steers his course accordingly."

Rabanus reads it allegorically, John and the prophets being "the voice going before the Word", so that "when prophecy ceased and was fettered, then came the Word". Gill supplies the fact the others leave vague, naming the prison from Josephus as the castle of Machaerus. Calvin ends on Luke's phrase rather than Matthew's, that Jesus came into Galilee in the power of the Spirit, and presses what it guards: we must not "imagine Christ to have any thing about him that is earthly or human".
13:
Matthew says only that he left Nazareth, and Ellicott is careful to note it: "St. Matthew records the bare fact." Everyone else supplies the reason from Luke — the townsmen had rejected him and tried to throw him from the brow of the hill. Clarke presses the verb, which is compounded with an intensive, into "entirely leaving Nazareth", so that Christ "utterly forsook" the place; Wesley says the same in a line; Gill notes he had preached there first, and to their liking, before it turned.

Lightfoot alone counts the years and grieves over them. Jesus had passed "six or seven-and-twenty years there", and after this "we do not read that he returned thither again; and so, unhappy Nazareth, thou perishest by thine own folly and perverseness."

Why Capernaum is answered most fully by Ellicott, who gives four reasons. Its position on the lake, with a garrison and a custom-house, made it the natural centre of the fishing trade, which suited the four disciples already partly settled there. It lay within an easy day's journey of Nazareth, so that return visits, and visits from his mother and brethren, remained possible. It held publicans and Gentiles of a kind "not to be found in the more secluded villages". And the healing of the officer's son had already "secured there a certain degree of protection and of influence". Robertson compresses all this into a comparison: in Capernaum the message "would have a better chance than in Jerusalem with its ecclesiastical prejudices or in Nazareth with its local jealousies".

Where the city actually stood can be watched being discovered across three commentaries. Barnes, writing earliest, says the site "is now uncertain", and reports an American missionary finding in 1823 only twenty or thirty uninhabited Arab huts among the presumed ruins. Ellicott can report that the Palestine Exploration Society has identified it with Tell-Hûm and disinterred a Roman-period building thought to be the synagogue — "possibly, therefore, the very synagogue, built by the believing centurion, in which our Lord worshipped and taught". Robertson, later still, gives the identification as settled.

Lightfoot then answers a question the others only raise. Capernaum is called Christ's own city, and it was there he paid the half-shekel; why? Because Jewish law made residence into citizenship by a graduated scale, which he quotes: thirty days in a city makes a man liable to the alms-chest, six months to clothing the poor, nine months (the Babylonian Gemara adds) to burying them, and twelve months to the ordinary tributes and taxes — "how long does a man dwell in some city before he be as one of the citizens? Twelve months." Clarke borrows the rule from him without disguise.

Calvin reads the move as a deliberate withdrawal rather than a migration: Christ had been accustomed to frequent Nazareth, and now "in order to avoid danger, he now bade a final adieu to it". On the phrase that gives the district its name he is more careful than most, explaining that Galilee is called of the Gentiles "not only on account of its vicinity to Tyre and Sidon, but because its inhabitants were a mixture of Jews and Gentiles" — and then correcting his own reference in the same sentence, since the cities granted to King Hiram were a gift not of David but of Solomon.

The lesser details are agreed. Barnes fixes the town on the north-west corner of the lake and lists the miracles worked there, remarking that Jesus spent "no small part of the three years of his public ministry" in the neighbourhood; Clarke observes that Capernaum is famous throughout the New Testament and never mentioned in the Old, guessing it one of the cities built after the return from Babylon; Ellicott notes that the older manuscripts spell the abandoned town Nazara.
14:
Calvin alone admits the quotation is a problem: "there is some appearance, as if Matthew had put a wrong meaning on the quotation from the prophet." His defence is to read Isaiah in context. Two calamities had fallen — Tiglath-Pileser carrying off the northern tribes, Shalmaneser finishing the kingdom — and a third, worse, was foretold; against that the promise is that the last dimness will be less than the first. He rejects confining it to Jerusalem's escape from Sennacherib as "very absurd", makes the return from Babylon the dawn and Christ the sunrise, and concludes that "our souls are plunged in the darkness of everlasting death, till he enlightens them by his grace". Barnes puts the technical point plainly: Matthew "has given the sense, but not the very words".

The best small observation belongs to Clarke. Isaiah wrote that the people walked in darkness; Matthew writes that they sat in it. He takes the change as deliberate — sitting "expresses a greater degree of intellectual blindness, than walking in darkness does" — and infers that after seven centuries they were worse off than when the prophet spoke. Wesley builds a three-step descent from the same words: "first, they walked, then they sat in darkness, and lastly, in the region of the shadow of death."

On that last phrase Barnes and Clarke converge independently. A shadow requires a body between the ground and the sun; so Barnes has death standing between the nations and the light, and Clarke "Death's country, where, in a peculiar manner, Death lived, reigned, and triumphed".

Why the district was called Galilee of the Gentiles is agreed but variously sourced: Clarke cites Strabo for Egyptians, Arabians and Phoenicians, Barnes upper Galilee's neighbourhood with Tyre and Sidon. On "beyond Jordan" they part company — Barnes insists it does not mean east of the river but near it, perhaps near its sources, while Wesley assumes the eastward sense Barnes denies.

Two voices independently report the same fact: the Jews expected the Messiah to appear first in Galilee. Gill says the expectation "must be grounded on this prophecy"; Clarke calls it "a regular tradition among the ancient Jews", citing Schoetgen for proofs.

Barnes takes the darkness as social too. Galileans were proverbially ignorant, marked by "a coarse, outlandish manner of speech" — whence his point: "it shows the great compassion of the Saviour, that he went to preach to such poor and despised sinners. Instead of seeking the rich and the learned, he chose to minister to the needy, the ignorant, and the contemned."

What "began to preach" means is disputed, since by every account he had preached before. Gill dates it not from Capernaum nor from John's arrest but "from the time that Satan left tempting him"; Wesley and Robertson make it the start of settled public work, Robertson noting he "had been preaching for over a year already elsewhere". Ellicott puts a season on it, the autumn or winter between the Passovers of A.D. 26 and 27, and describes the method from Luke: read the prophetic lesson, make it the text, preach repentance and forgiveness, announce the kingdom as near rather than far off.

That the opening words are the Baptist's own is noticed by all. Gill takes it as proof of entire agreement, the two preaching "not only the same doctrine, but in the same words"; Wesley explains why they could not change, since "the repentance which John taught still was, and ever will be, the necessary preparation"; Clarke makes it a rule for every commissioned preacher. Pseudo-Chrysostom ties the beginning to what preceded — the gospel belongs to one who has overcome hunger in the desert, despised covetousness on the mountain and rejected ambition in the temple — and Cyril draws the lesson of timing: if the Master "followed the right time in due order, ought we, His servants, to venture out of order?"
18:
Read alone the call is abrupt, as Ellicott says: "in no part of the Gospel history is it more necessary to remember St. John's record as we read that of the Three." From the fourth Gospel he reconstructs their previous life — the sons of Jona and of Zebedee growing up at Bethsaida as partners, their national hopes quickened by the rising of Judas of Galilee, then baptised by John, pointed to the Lamb of God, and for a time his companions. Simon had already been given his new name. Henry agrees, and draws the lesson: "Christ brings poor souls by degrees into fellowship with himself."

What happened next Ellicott states plainly and Calvin would not allow. On Ellicott's account, when Christ began his Galilean circuit "He was alone, and left them to return to their old calling", uncertain whether he would want them again — exactly the situation Calvin uses to disprove a prior call: if they had been called and gone back to the boats, "it would follow that they were apostates, who had forsaken their Master, despised their calling". Both cannot stand.

Whether Luke records the same occasion is disputed more courteously. Ellicott notes Matthew and Mark "agree almost verbally" while Luke "presents more difficulty", and inclines to one event fully told. Calvin argues it at length and draws a general principle: "no fixed and distinct order of dates was observed" by the evangelists, who "disregard the order of time" and present "the leading transactions" in summary.

Why the first ministers were fishermen produces the sharpest modern quarrel. Clarke asks why not the eminent scribes: since the teaching had to come from above, mean instruments made plain that "the excellency of the power" was of God. He then turns it on his own day's institutions: seminaries have real uses, but "to make preachers of the Gospel is a matter to which they are utterly inadequate; it is a prerogative that God never did, and never will, delegate to man", and "men-made ministers have almost ruined the heritage of God".

Henry, from the same premise, guards the opposite flank. Christ "sometimes chooses to endow those with the gifts of grace who have least to show of the gifts of nature" — then the qualification Clarke never makes: "yet this will not justify the bold intrusion of ignorant and unqualified men into the work of the ministry." His interest is where the call was issued: not to Herod's court, not to the chief priests, but to a lake in a despised province, so "surely Christ sees not as man sees". They were poor, he observes, for a man with an estate does not make fishing his trade.

Lightfoot supplies the law under which they worked. Among the ten conditions the rabbis credit to Joshua was that any Israelite might "spread his nets for fishing in the sea of Tiberias" — but under a caution, that none set up a wall obstructing shipping, since fishermen liked to drive stakes and build cane fences, "not permitted, because it is an impediment to the ships". Though the sea lay in Naphtali's portion it was open to all.

Robertson attends to the tackle: the word here is a casting-net, thrown over the shoulder to open in a circle, while two verses later a general word appears and the great drag-net waits for a later chapter. Barnes describes the water — fifteen miles long, stormy from the surrounding hills, its shores called by Josephus "a perfect paradise". Henry adds the rabbinic compliment that of all the seas God chose none but Gennesaret.

Pseudo-Chrysostom explains the timing: the apostles were called "before He spoke or did any thing", so no word or deed should be hidden from them and they could afterwards say, "what we have seen and heard, that we cannot but speak". Their trade, he adds, was a prophecy of their future work.
19:
Ellicott hears in the summons something larger: it was "in some sense the first parable in our Lord's teaching" — the sea the evil world, souls the fish, the net the Church. The figure existed already in Jeremiah, but there "it had presented its darker aspect, and the 'fishers of men' were their captors and enslavers"; its happier use he traces to the earliest surviving Christian hymn, where Clement addresses Christ as "Fisher of men, the blest, / Out of the world's unrest, / Out of sin's troubled sea / Taking us, Lord, to Thee." Clarke prefers Ezekiel's healed waters as the allusion.

Gill and Lightfoot both find the same phrase in Maimonides, "a fisher of the law", which Gill uses to mark the difference: Christ "made them not fishers of the law, but fishers of the Gospel".

Clarke turns the metaphor against unfit ministers. Only those God fits are called, and "miserable are those who do not wait for this call — who presume to take the name of fishers of men, and know not how to cast the net of the Divine word": such men "study not to catch men, but to catch money". He quotes Fletcher at them: "Some will be eyes, but have no light to see; / Some will be guides, but have no feet to go... / Dumb, deaf, lame, blind, and maimed, yet fishers all!" On the summons he is gentler, noting that most divine calls come "in a few solemn words, which alarm the conscience, and deeply impress the heart".

Whether these men were strangers is settled the same way by both who raise it. Gill has them formerly John's disciples who spent a day with Christ, returned to their master, and after his imprisonment "betook themselves to their former employment"; Robertson notes they were already disciples. Both accept the sequence Calvin refused.

What the leaving cost Clarke defends against a sneer. Some object that men with only nets sacrificed little; his answer is that "he who has nothing but a net, and leaves that for the sake of doing good to the souls of men, leaves his All", and that a man who lived comfortably by it may afterwards "want even a morsel of bread". Barnes reaches the point by imagination — "little did they know what awaited them, when they left their unmended nets to rot on the beach, and followed the unknown and unhonoured Jesus of Nazareth". Gill totals what went too: boats, trade, substance, relations, friends.

Ellicott refuses an apologetic argument available to him. If Luke's incident came first, the mending here would follow from the breaking there, "and be noted as an undesigned coincidence" — but he declines it twice: mending and washing followed even an unsuccessful night, and Luke's Greek says the nets were on the point of breaking, not that they broke. Robertson keeps to the verb, which means adjusting: they were getting their gear ready.

Leaving the father draws the sharpest pastoral writing. Clarke states the competing duty first — after God, provision for parents "is the highest duty we owe" — then subordinates it: when God calls to the ministry, "father and mother and all must be left", and if their support is not otherwise made up "it is a proof we have mistaken our call". His closing turn is unexpected: what an honour the vocation was to old Zebedee, who, if pious, must have felt "unutterable delight". Ellicott reads the detail sociologically: Mark's hired servants suggest the sons of Zebedee were better off than the sons of Jona, whose father's absence may mean he was dead.

Calvin declines to explain the promptness psychologically. What strikes him is "the power of Christ's voice" — not the voice alone, since "those whom the Lord is pleased to lead and draw to himself, are inwardly addressed by his Spirit".
23:
Pseudo-Chrysostom explains the order: kings gather an army before war, so the Lord "first collected Apostles, and then began to preach the Gospel"; and since the sick "could not come to their physician, He as a zealous Physician went about to visit" them. Robertson counts this the first of three Galilean circuits — four fishermen now, the twelve next, then the twelve sent ahead in pairs.

The word synagogue sends three into research, and they disagree on its age. Barnes calls the origin "involved in much obscurity": only sacrifice was confined to Jerusalem, so other worship could happen anywhere, and the need for shelter from storm and heat produced the buildings. Clarke dates them after the return from Babylon, and adds a detail nobody else has: they were built "especially by rivers, that they might have water for the convenience of their frequent washings". Both report four hundred and eighty in Jerusalem and the same rule of ten men, which Lightfoot traces to the Talmud: a great city is one with ten men of leisure, and "if there be less than this number, behold, it is a village". Barnes adds the custom that matters: the reader stood and the expounder sat, so "our Saviour imitated their example, and was commonly seated".

Four voices converge on the same distinction between the words for illness, Robertson stating it briefly. Clarke quotes Theophylact for a chronic disorder against "a temporary disorder of the body", insisting the difference "is necessary to be observed"; Ellicott extends the scale, the "torments" of the next verse implying something more acute; Henry gives examples of all three — blindness and fever, fluxes and consumptions, gout and convulsions.

Calvin's note on the lunatics is the chapter's most surprising. He explains the Greek from the moon and admits Greeks, Romans and Jews alike supposed such disorders followed its phases — then declines to let the Bible be held responsible. "Scripture was not intended to determine questions of physical science, in which inductive reasoning is a sufficient guide, but to declare those truths, which could never have been known without an express revelation." The word no more commits the sacred writers to lunar medicine than talk of sunrise commits us to believing the sun moves and not the earth. He is as careful with the demoniacs, distinct from all merely troubled by the devil: the term belongs to those given up to Satan so that "he holds possession of their minds and of their bodily senses".

What the healings were for divides Calvin from Ellicott. For Calvin they are proof: such diseases "cannot be healed by natural means", so curing them "proved his divinity". Ellicott resists that emphasis: Matthew records them "not directly as evidence of a supernatural mission, but almost, so to speak, as the natural accompaniments of His work; signs, not of power only or chiefly, but of the love, tenderness, pity, which were the true marks... of the kingdom of heaven". Calvin is scrupulous about scope: not everyone diseased was cured, but "there was no class of diseases, that was ever presented to him, which he did not" heal.

Henry presses the physician image hardest. Some illnesses "are called the reproach of physicians, being obstinate to all the methods they can prescribe; but even those were the glory of this Physician", his word "the true panpharmacon". He reads the three named afflictions as covering everything: palsy the greatest weakness of body, lunacy of mind, possession the greatest calamity of both. The crowds he explains by the terms — a physician "so easy of access, so sure of success", who "cured gratis, and took no fees, could not but have abundance of patients" — noting that Christ "might have issued out a proclamation to summon all to come to him", and went instead. Wesley adds that gospel means the joyous message, "the proper name of our religion".
24:
How far the fame reached is measured carefully. Barnes admits it is "not easy to fix the exact bounds" of Syria; Wesley calls it the whole province, "of which the Jewish country was only a small part". Ellicott takes the word popularly rather than as the Roman province, and adds that the ministry itself stayed within Palestine but for one journey, the wider fame showing in hearers from Idumaea and Tyre and in disciples at Damascus soon after the Ascension. Robertson reaches for a modern comparison: rumour "carries things almost like the wireless or radio", so that "Jesus had a moving hospital of patients".

Robertson opens the vocabulary: the sick are literally "those who had it bad", and torments began as a touchstone, the Lydian stone that tested gold, before meaning examination by torture. Clarke gives the same root and names colics and gout, "which racked every joint".

On the demoniacs the question is whether the evangelists meant it. Barnes states the alternative fairly — that the phrase denoted only the melancholy or epileptic — then argues against it in seven steps: Christ and the apostles managed them as persons; they spoke, answered and confessed knowledge of Christ, which "could not be said of diseases"; they went out and entered others; they were named, threatened and silenced; the fathers read the accounts so; and if Christ's belief here may be denied, no other sentiment of his is safe. Clarke sides with him, naming and rejecting the theory "that the sacred writers accommodated themselves to the unfounded prejudices of the common people" — an explanation that "can never comport with the accounts given of these persons". Ellicott defers the question to the Gadarene narrative, noting only that the word here is demon, not the word used of the Tempter, and that the possessed are grouped with the lunatics yet distinguished from them.

Clarke presses the grammatical half harder. The English plural "devils" is wrong, since the Greek word "is not found in the plural in any part of the Sacred Writings, when speaking of evil spirits": demons are many, the Devil one and supreme.

The moon divides them three ways. Clarke defends the old belief as true, since at new and full moon sun and moon act together on the atmosphere, producing tides and, in sensitive constitutions, real change. Barnes keeps the name and drops the theory: it was given "because it was formerly imagined" the disease followed the moon, "although it is not certain that the moon has any effect", on which "physicians are not determined, but no harm arises from the use of the name". Ellicott reports the belief, noting that Eastern travellers dreaded a stroke of moon almost as much as of sun.

On the palsy Ellicott is precise: the word "points, not to a view of the cause of the disease, but to its conspicuous phenomena" — lost muscular control and looseness of limb.

The crowds Clarke reads as a fulfilment the Jews would have recognised, expecting the Messiah's days to answer the famine of Amos — "not a famine of bread, but of hearing the words of the Lord" — and multitudes to gather to the one who dispensed it. Gill quotes the rabbinic rule that "there is no multitude less than sixty myriads", then warns against taking it literally. Robertson notes the plural, "not just one crowd, but crowds and crowds".

Decapolis produces a last disagreement of fact. Clarke calls Damascus its metropolis and most ancient city, and puts the district on both sides of Jordan; Barnes makes Scythopolis chief and the only one west of the river, Damascus merely a possible member; Ellicott, giving Pliny's list, notes that Josephus's calling Scythopolis the largest makes it "almost certain that he did not include Damascus" at all. Barnes adds what explains a later story: these cities were chiefly Greek, "hence the keeping of swine".
